mcqs.question: What is the core mechanism of the bulkhead pattern for isolating a slow dependency?
options: Retrying every failed call up to 3 times before giving up
Caching every response from the dependency to avoid calling it again
Giving each dependency its own bounded resource pool, so one dependency running slow can only exhaust its own allocation
Increasing the shared thread pool's total size so nothing ever runs out
mcqs.explanation: Bulkheading bounds and separates resource consumption per dependency, capping the blast radius of any one dependency's slowdown. Retries and caching don't address shared-pool exhaustion, and simply growing the shared pool just delays the same problem at higher scale rather than isolating it.

mcqs.question: A service shares a 100-thread pool between a fast cache and a slow third-party API. When the third-party API degrades from 200ms to 30s per call, why do cache calls start failing too?
options: The cache itself becomes slower whenever any other dependency degrades
All 100 threads fill up waiting on the slow API, leaving no free threads for the unrelated cache calls to run on
The load balancer automatically routes cache calls to the third-party API during a slowdown
The database underlying the cache crashes whenever thread usage rises
mcqs.explanation: With no dedicated pool, every thread can end up blocked on the slow dependency, so unrelated cache calls have nowhere to run even though the cache itself is perfectly healthy. The cache's own speed doesn't change, there's no such load-balancer behavior, and the database isn't affected by thread pool exhaustion in another part of the service.

mcqs.question: What do bulkheads trade away in exchange for a hard ceiling on blast radius?
options: Some resource utilization, since a dependency's reserved pool sits idle when it's healthy and capacity is needed elsewhere
Correctness — bulkheaded calls can return wrong results
The ability to monitor the dependency's health at all
Compatibility with circuit breakers on the same dependency
mcqs.explanation: Reserved capacity for one dependency can't be borrowed by others even when it's sitting idle and they're under load — that's the average-case cost paid for a guaranteed worst-case bound. Bulkheads don't affect result correctness, don't block health monitoring, and work alongside circuit breakers rather than conflicting with them.

mcqs.question: Does a bulkhead replace the need for a circuit breaker on the same dependency?
options: Yes, a bulkhead makes a circuit breaker fully redundant
Yes, but only for dependencies with fewer than 10 concurrent callers
No, because bulkheads and circuit breakers cannot be applied to the same dependency simultaneously
No — the bulkhead caps damage from calls already in flight, while the breaker stops new calls once the dependency is clearly failing; use both
mcqs.explanation: They address different moments in a failure: the bulkhead limits how much in-flight calls can consume, and the breaker prevents new calls from being sent once failure is detected — together they cover more than either alone. They aren't mutually exclusive, aren't redundant, and there's no caller-count rule limiting when both can apply.
